body.x: Few questions in a rishta process cause as much quiet anxiety as this one. The mehr must be named before the nikah, it will be written into the contract, and yet almost nobody tells families how to choose the amount. Set it too high and it looks like a price tag; set it too low and someone whispers that the bride was undervalued. The truth is less dramatic: there is no correct figure, only a figure that fits the couple, their circumstances, and the purpose the mehr is meant to serve in their marriage. This guide is about finding that fit.
Decide what the mehr is for, before deciding what it is

The Qur'an presents the mehr as the bride's own due — her property, given to her and not to her father or family, and hers to keep, spend or freely remit. Within that fixed principle, families in practice use the mehr in two different ways. For some it is symbolic: a modest amount whose role is to mark the seriousness of the contract. For others it is security: a substantial sum, most of it usually deferred, intended to give the wife real financial standing if the marriage ends. Neither approach is more religious than the other, and scholars do not publish a tariff. But the two intentions lead to very different numbers, so the first task — for the bride and her wali, privately — is to say out loud which of the two this mehr is meant to be, or what blend of the two.
The three anchors families actually use
When families settle on a figure calmly, they are usually — without naming it — weighing the same three anchors:

The first anchor is the groom's real means: his income, his debts and his obligations. A deferred mehr he could never actually pay protects no one; it is decoration, not security. The second is custom in your own community — what families around you, in your city and your tradition, ordinarily set. Custom is a recognised reference point in Islamic law, and a figure wildly out of line with it will draw comment whatever its merits. The third is the bride's own circumstances: her age, her earnings, whether she has been married before, and what support she would realistically have if the marriage ended.
A figure that survives all three anchors — payable by him, ordinary in your community, meaningful for her — is almost always a defensible one.
The examples below are invented, and the amounts in them are round illustrations, not recommendations and not norms. What matters is the reasoning, which is real.

Household one: a couple in their early twenties in Birmingham, both at the start of modest jobs, marrying with both families' support close at hand. They choose the symbolic route: a small prompt amount — illustratively, a few hundred pounds — paid at the nikah, and a deferred portion set at a level the groom could genuinely raise within a year if he had to. Their reasoning is that they are building a life together from very little, and neither wants the contract to open with a heavy debt hanging over it.

Household two: a groom in his mid-thirties in Toronto with an established career, and a bride who will leave her job and relocate to his city. Her family asks for security, and he agrees readily: a modest prompt amount, and a deferred mehr — illustratively, a sum in the tens of thousands — that reflects what she is giving up and would let her restart independently if the marriage failed. The figure is high because the risk it covers is real, and because he can honestly stand behind it.

Household three: a second marriage in Houston, both parties in their forties, with children and assets of their own. They set the mehr partly in gold, a traditional form in their family, at a value both consider dignified rather than strategic, and they record separate written understandings about the property each of them already owns. Their reasoning: at their stage of life, clarity matters more than size.
The mistakes that distort the number

Status bidding: matching or beating the figure from a wealthier family's wedding, as if the mehr were a public ranking.
Copying a cousin's number: importing a figure set for different incomes, a different city and a different intention, without importing the reasoning behind it.
Leaving it to the nikah week: a conversation held under time pressure, in front of relatives, becomes a negotiation nobody enjoys and somebody quietly resents.
Setting an unpayable deferred sum: a number chosen for how it sounds when read aloud, which teaches both sides that contract terms are theatre.
Trading it against other things: letting the mehr become a bargaining counter for the venue, the guest list or the rukhsati date.
A calm method for settling it early

The bride and her wali agree the intention — symbolic, security, or a blend — and a range they would accept, before any number is spoken to the other side.
The subject is raised early, usually through the same elder or intermediary carrying the rishta, around the second serious conversation — not at the engagement, and never first at the nikah itself.
Prompt and deferred portions are decided separately and deliberately: what is paid at the contract, and what is recorded as her deferred right.
If the two sides open far apart, negotiate the reasoning before the figure: ask what the number is meant to do, and let the amount follow from the answer.
Once agreed, the amount is written exactly into the nikah nama and the subject is closed — not reopened at the rukhsati, and not used as leverage in later disagreements.

If a family is unsure whether a proposed figure or condition is valid, a scholar or their marja's office will advise, and that advice is worth taking before the contract rather than after it. On Shia Rishta, profiles deliberately carry no mehr field — it is a family conversation, not a listing detail. But the couples who handle it best share one habit: they treat the mehr as the bride's right and the groom's word, and they settle it early, quietly, and once.

excerpt: There is no official figure for mehr — but there is a calm, honest way for two families to reach a number that protects the bride without burdening the groom.
title: How much mehr is appropriate? A practical guide
